say.text: Last stretch. You build the one-pager, and I only hand you facts to explain.
Each time, pick the reason behind the fact. Reasons stick; lists fade.
**Fact:** TOF is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**, yet no two children present alike.
Which reason best explains the variation?

choices.label: How severe the RVOT obstruction is

say.text: Yes. Presentation varies with the severity of **RVOT obstruction**.
Hold that idea. It runs the whole one-pager.
Tempting: the VSD is the hole you can see. But the source ties presentation to the severity of **RVOT obstruction**.

sure_note: You were sure, so lock this in: obstruction sets the picture, not the hole.

say.text: **Fact:** classic TOF has exactly four components.
Which set is the right one-liner?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH
VSD, ASD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH

say.text: Right: a **large, anteriorly malaligned VSD**, an **overriding aorta**, **infundibular RVOT obstruction** and **RVH**.
ASD tempts because it is another septal hole. But it is not among the four.
The four are the VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and RVH.

sure_note: You were sure, so note it: ASD is not a component of classic TOF.

say.text: PDA tempts because it sits in so many congenital lists. But it is not among the four.
The four are the VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and RVH.

sure_note: You were sure, so note it: PDA is not a component of classic TOF.

say.text: LVH tempts because 'hypertrophy' is the familiar word. The ventricle in classic TOF is the right one.
The four include **right ventricular hypertrophy**.

sure_note: You were sure, so note it: it is RVH, never LVH, in the four.

say.text: **Fact:** **Pentalogy of Fallot** is a named variant. The term is old and seldom used now.
What is the fifth part?
Yes. Pentalogy = TOF plus an **atrial septal defect**.
PDA tempts because it is the other classic extra shunt. But pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus an **atrial septal defect**.
**Fact:** with significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Pick the reason this makes a child blue.

choices.label: Most blood skips the lungs and heads to the aorta
A bigger VSD leaks more, whatever the RVOT does

say.text: Follow the blood. Right ventricular blood has two exits: the RVOT or across the VSD to the aorta. A tight RVOT in front of it changes which exit it takes.
Yes. Now flip it: if RVOT resistance is less than systemic vascular resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Tempting: the VSD is the visible hole. But colour is set by what the blood meets at the RVOT. With significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta.
Try again with the RVOT in mind.

sure_note: You were sure, so this one pays off: the hole does not set the colour, the obstruction does.

say.text: Same idea, new angle. RVOT resistance is **less** than systemic vascular resistance.
How cyanotic is the child?

choices.label: Deeply blue, since the VSD is large

say.text: Yes. Low RVOT resistance relative to the body means little cyanosis. High RVOT resistance sends most blood toward the aorta.
VSD size tempts, but it is not the rule. If RVOT resistance is below systemic resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
With significant obstruction, most blood bypasses the lungs.
**Fact:** the chest radiograph may classically show a **boot-shaped heart**, with an upturned apex due to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Pick the reason it looks like a boot.

choices.label: The whole heart is simply enlarged

say.text: Yes. The **upturned apex** comes from right ventricular hypertrophy.
'Boot' sounds big, so cardiomegaly tempts. But the source names a different cause: an upturned apex due to RVH.
LV is the heart's usual hypertrophy story, so it tempts. But in classic TOF the hypertrophy is right ventricular, and that lifts the apex.
The boot is a classic sign. Which investigation is the gold standard for diagnosis?
Yes. The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard and the primary diagnostic modality.
The boot is vivid and exam-famous, so it tempts. But a classic sign is not the gold standard. That is the **echocardiogram**.

sure_note: You were sure, so remember: boot = classic X-ray sign, echo = gold standard.

say.text: A child with TOF is in a tet spell. First step: **knee-chest positioning**.
Why does it help?

choices.label: It lowers systemic resistance so blood flows on
It clears fluid from the lungs, like in heart failure

say.text: Recall: cyanosis depends on the RVOT resistance compared with systemic resistance. Which side of that balance can you change by moving the child's legs?
Yes. Knee-chest positioning raises **systemic vascular resistance**.
Vasodilating tempts if you think 'open the circuit'. But the source gives the opposite aim: knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance.
Try once more.

sure_note: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: spell steps raise systemic resistance, they do not lower it.

say.text: The heart-failure reflex tempts. But the step is about resistance, not lung fluid: knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance.
Try once more.

sure_note: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a spell is not heart failure, so no diuretic reflex.

say.text: Different angle. The RVOT-versus-systemic resistance balance sets how blue the child is.
Which change helps?
Yes. **Knee-chest** increases systemic vascular resistance.
Lowering it is tempting, but it is the reverse of the aim. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance.
Phenylephrine does the same job by drug.
Next in a spell: **IV fluid boluses**.

choices.label: Fluids are unsafe, so give a diuretic instead

say.text: Yes. Boluses are given to improve **RV filling**.
Diuretic tempts if you file this under heart failure. But the source gives **IV fluid boluses**, to improve RV filling.

choices.label: IV beta-blocker: speeds the heart to force blood past the RVOT

say.text: Yes. **Phenylephrine** increases systemic afterload.
Spell kit: knee-chest, oxygen, fluids, beta-blockers, phenylephrine, with morphine as sedative.
Speeding the heart sounds like pushing harder. But **IV beta-blockers** decrease heart rate and aid RV filling.
Phenylephrine is the one that increases systemic afterload.
Oxygen is the familiar first reflex, so it tempts. Its reason here is **pulmonary vasodilation**, not lowering systemic resistance.
Phenylephrine is the one that increases systemic afterload.
